title: Boundary tension examples — labeling scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad to capture weird/borderline examples we keep hitting in the users dataset. Not a final guideline — use this for triage + lightweight adjudication and to seed a short rubric for the next annotation pass.

Scope:
- Short text field sources: support chat snippets, product feedback, small bios, OCRed receipts.
- Focus: entity boundary decisions and cleanup rules where labelers disagree.

Quick glossary (labels I use in notes):
- ORG, PRODUCT, PERSON, ID (product SKU / internal id), ERROR_CODE, QUANTITY, DATE, PHONE, ABBREV, URL, MISC

Core heuristics (working rules, subject to change):
1) Keep minimal contiguous spans that convey the entity. If a punctuation or parenthetical is part of official name (™ / ® / ©) keep it, otherwise strip for PRODUCT/ORG.
   - Example: “Acme Co., Inc.” -> label ORG: Acme Co. (drop trailing punctuation unless the data consumer expects exact legal form)
2) Numeric suffixes attached to letters: treat as ID when they follow known SKU patterns (letters+hyphen+digits). Else treat as part of product name if marketed that way.
   -  "XJ-400" -> ID;  "Model XJ-400 Pro" -> PRODUCT: Model XJ-400 Pro (span includes model modifier)
3) Hyphen tension: if hyphen joins two nouns that together form a single marketed phrase, annotate whole span; if hyphen is connector in a list, split.
   -  "state-of-the-art" in product title -> PRODUCT span includes whole phrase
   -  "blue-green/red" in color list -> two spans (blue-green and red) unless the UI treats them as one token.
4) URLs and code-like tokens: label as URL or ERROR_CODE/ID and do not try to normalize. Preserve partial truncations (e.g., example.com/… ) as-is.
5) Parentheticals: prefer excluding explanatory parentheticals unless they disambiguate (e.g., chemical formula, SKU).
   -  "WidgetPlus (v2)" -> PRODUCT: WidgetPlus (v2) OR PRODUCT: WidgetPlus and ID: v2? Flag for adjudication if downstream needs versioning.
6) Emails and handles: treat as CONTACT only when context expects contact info; otherwise MISC.

Representative examples (raw -> label decision -> rationale / next action):
- "ordered 2x Model-Mini-3 (blue) on 1/12/25" -> QUANTITY: 2x | PRODUCT: Model-Mini-3 | MISC: (blue) | DATE: 1/12/25
  Rationale: quantity tokens attached to verbs should be separate. Keep parentheses as MISC unless product color is needed for fulfilment.

- "invoice# 0001234-AB (acct: acme_corp)" -> ID: 0001234-AB | ORG: acme_corp
  Rationale: invoice numbers follow digits+alpha, mark as ID. Lowercase underscore org handles — normalize to display form in cleanup pass.

- "error: EOF_ERR_110 at line 432" -> ERROR_CODE: EOF_ERR_110 | MISC: line 432
  Rationale: code-like tokens are stable signals for QA.

- "Dr. Luis Mª Ortega" -> PERSON: Luis Mª Ortega (keep accent/abbrev)
  Rationale: preserve diacritics and honorifics inside PERSON span; strip honorific to separate PERSON token only if downstream requires full name normalization.

- "promo: buy1-get1@amazon.com" -> MISC or PRODUCT? -> label MISC (ambiguous mashed token), flag for cleanup to split email-like token later.

- "SKU: 88--A / 88-A" -> ID: 88-A (normalize double-dash to single)
  Action: add a small cleanup rule to collapse repeated punctuation in SKU fields (but keep proof in raw field).

- "Café/Bar — La Nueva ™" -> PRODUCT: La Nueva ™ | MISC: Café/Bar (contextual: if full business name is "Café/Bar La Nueva" then ORG=full).

Cross-lingual and OCR oddities:
- Spaces inside words from OCR: "libra ry" -> attempt auto-merge if confidence low but include original raw_text in metadata.
- Slashed languages: "en/es: thanks / gracias" -> label two separate phrases; language detection helps splitting.

Adjudication shortcuts (for quick reviewer decisions):
- If labelers differ only on punctuation inclusion (comma, period, trailing ®/™), choose the span without punctuation and record exception if legal-name required.
- If one labeler marked PRODUCT vs ORG and word tokenization suggests company-product ambiguity, prefer PRODUCT in UI/product context; ORG in corporate/contact context.
- Use "split and tie" pattern: annotate overlapping spans (both PRODUCT and ID) with short reason code when necessary, but avoid training overlap unless we plan multi-label.

Sampling ideas for second-pass cleaning:
- Prioritize items with high labeler disagreement (kappa < 0.6).
- Sample by tokens containing special characters (@ / # ™ ® % + =) and by tokens with digits+letters mixture.
- Add a focused batch of OCR-eyes (low-confidence OCR pages) and multilingual short tweets.

Lightweight normalization checklist (for cleanup pipeline, not annotation):
- NFKC normalization
- Collapse repeated punctuation (but store raw)
- Map common optical confusions (0/O, 1/I, l/1) in ID-only contexts using conservative heuristics
- Lowercase normalization for free-text search fields, but preserve case for PERSON/ORG/PRODUCT canonicalization

Open questions / TODOs (flagged for triage):
- Do we need a distinct label for VERSION vs ID? Many dataset consumers request version as a structured field. (Jira: INF-1249)
- How to deal with sloppily concatenated tokens from chat paste (e.g., "refundplease123") — split heuristics will break proper nouns. Need a regex whitelist.
- Agree on a canonical strategy for parentheses containing brand suffixes: include or split?

Notas personales / quick notes to self:
- Try running the small cleanup rules on 5k random support rows and measure how many label spans change.
- Build a tiny adjudication UI clip: show raw, auto-normalized candidate, labeler span A/B, and comment field. Keep it lightweight (no full pipeline).
- Add 10 high-disagreement examples to shared folder for training overhaul.

Reference links / tickets:
- INF-1249: versioning vs id split (see linked artifacts)
- Slack thread: #annotation-weirdness (search for "boundary tension")

Final note: this is effectively a living scratchpad. The priority is to capture weird examples and the minimal rationales so we can later distill into a 1-page rubric for labelers. Don't overformalize here.
